title: Need some advice on how to optimize my AI Game
author: thousandlytales
selftext:
My game is powered by AI API (deepinfra or other services). I do doublecheck the service ToS to make sure that they don't store and sell their user data ofc. The problem is that currently to make my AI game work I need to send a very large number of AI prompts per user action/inputs! One prompt to validate user input (make sure its not gibberish, offensive, explicit and so on), one prompt to actually predict the game's next output and actions, one prompt to determine the scene and character facial expressions to show, and one prompt to make sure the AI output isn't gibberish, offensive, or explicit.

So every time the user does an action it costs me 4-5 AI prompts which means I'll go bankrupt very quickly Q.Q

I've tried to combine the prompts ofc, but this leads to the AI ignoring parts of the prompt (as I'm using smaller models like llama3-8b and not the super expensive ones like chatgpt or claude). Pls help I don't have any kidneys left to sell to keep my game runnin.

comments.author: thousandlytales
comments.body: Before the convo shifts towards local AI, I've done some research and its simply not possible for over 99.9% of users as they would need at least a 4090 or a GPU with 24GB VRAM. Using an AI API service allows the game to run on even phones or toasters, anything with a web browser. So rather than packing the extremely demanding AI models into my game I'm delegating it to AI API services.

replies.author: Shalcker
replies.body:
Perhaps you could use LLMs to create sets of expected inputs and outputs that can be cached and delivered without API calls - at least then your API bill will be one-time. Offensive and explicit can be done with keywords, and "gibberish" can be reduced to "anything that doesn't exist in your dictionary" (which would be very cheap!).

Of course that depends on how dynamic you want your game to be, and how many variations you can predict ahead of time.

You could also look at DeepSeek - as far as i'm aware they got cheapest API for their pretty decent model, that way you might go bankrupt slower.

replies.author: thousandlytales
replies.body: The problem with caching responses is that for each new choice, I'm basically branching the entire game universe! Every choice leads to the generation of a completely unique output with its own set of choices, so it gets untenable.

replies.author: Shalcker
replies.body:
If you want to have "freeform story" a la AI Dungeon then there is no way around having similar monetization (users paying for "energy" to do their inputs).

But more contained setups, like "Escape Rooms", or "Shopkeeper shop:, can be largely generated upfront.

Then if you could make LLM prompt with list of potential responses matching the situation (you could make it part of system prompt for each call) and make LLM ignore everything else; then entire thing could be done in single pass.

replies.author: thousandlytales
replies.body: yup, using AI to generate static assets and dialogue options would be the most straightforward way togo. But I want to use AI as a window to peer into entire fictional worlds, to allow people to experience and interact with the worlds that I create.

comments.author: constroyr
comments.body:
Remove the two prompts to determine whether the input and output is offensive and gibberish. Let users type in gibberish. Hardcode a list of banned terms the user can’t type in. And if they can’t type in offensive content, the model almost definitely won’t generate offensive content. 

As for the cost of the other two prompts, just launch it and see. If it’s too expensive, then take it down. But depending on how many people play, it might not be that expensive. And if you have a ton of people playing, you could cover the cost with monetization.

comments.author: c35683
comments.body:
Can you share any more details about the game or provide some screenshots? It's hard to tell what can be done differently without seeing it.

>I've tried to combine the prompts ofc, but this leads to the AI ignoring parts of the prompt

In my experience LLM's can handle multiple tasks pretty well if you request a specific format for the response, e.g.

    You are a game master in a text adventure game. User input will consist of actions taken by the player. For every action, provide a response in the following json format:
    {
    "what happens next": <Describe what happens in 2 paragraphs. Require the player to make a decision at the end.>,
    "scene to show": <peaceful hills/snowy mountain/dramatic battlefield>,
    "facial expression": <fear/anger/disgust/happiness/uwu>,
    "new actions the player can take:" [<action1>, <action2>, <action3>, <action4>]
    }

And you should end up with sections matching your different requirements, e.g.:

* "As you ask for advice on optimizing your AI Game, a wise old wizard appears before you. He offers you a magical scroll containing powerful algorithms and coding techniques that can enhance your game's AI capabilities. However, he warns you that using these advanced methods may come with unforeseen consequences. He urges you to choose wisely before proceeding. Will you accept the wizard's gift and risk the unknown, or will you seek a different path to improve your game?"
* "peaceful hills"
* "happiness"
* \["Accept the wizard's gift and implement the advanced algorithms", "Politely decline the wizard's offer and seek alternative ways to optimize the AI", "Ask the wizard for more information about the potential consequences", "Ignore the wizard and continue on your current path"\]

I'm not sure if this simple example is in line with what you're doing, but maybe it helps. If you're not afraid of sharing your prompts, you can message me via DM/chat, I have some experience with prompt engineering.

>(as I'm using smaller models like llama3-8b and not the super expensive ones like chatgpt or claude)

How much does llama3-8b cost, is the $0.20 per 1 million tokens quote I found online accurate? OpenAI's GPT 3.5 turbo costs $0.50 per 1M, maybe it's worth taking a look at it if it turns out you can reduce the number of calls by switching to a different model.

If the pricing depends on the number of tokens more than the number of calls, you can also save money by generating shorter responses to pay less, like asking for shorter answers if it's text, or asking for just a number instead of a full answer if there are multiple numbered options to choose from.

comments.author: adrixshadow
comments.body:
To be viable on release you need the players themselves subscribe and link their accounts to the game.

Ideally there would be standardization around a service that can work over multiple games from multiple developers.

In other words don't think just in terms of your game but around a community built around AI games.

comments.author: JD_2020
comments.body:
Think of your action tree like function calls. Fine tune a specialized gpt-3.5-turbo with function calls on your specific action graph (use GPT to generate you a bunch of different theoretical game states to build your training set).

With it structured in a way the base function call model already is well trained on, you’ll get much more precise and accurate actions being output from the mode and you can format inputs the same way.
